title: What is therapy, and how does it work?
citation: Wampold, B. E. (2015). How important are the common factors in psychotherapy? An update. World Psychiatry, 14(3), 270-277.
content:
What is therapy, and how does it work?

Therapy is a structured conversation with a trained mental health professional that helps people understand their thoughts, emotions, behaviours and experiences. Rather than giving advice or telling someone what to do, therapy helps people make sense of what they are going through, develop new ways of coping and create meaningful change over time. Different types of therapy use different techniques, but they all aim to improve wellbeing by helping people better understand themselves and respond more effectively to life's challenges.

Isn't therapy only for people with a serious problem?

A common misconception is that therapy is only for people experiencing a severe mental health condition or crisis. In reality, many people attend therapy to manage everyday stress, navigate life changes, improve relationships, build confidence, or better understand themselves. Just as people exercise to maintain their physical health, therapy can be a way of looking after mental and emotional wellbeing before problems become overwhelming.

Why does talking to someone actually help?

Talking can be helpful because putting thoughts and emotions into words allows the brain to organise experiences that may previously have felt confusing or overwhelming. A therapist also provides an objective perspective, helping people notice patterns, challenge unhelpful ways of thinking and explore situations from new angles. Over time, this process can reduce emotional distress and support healthier ways of coping, making change feel more achievable.

What actually happens in a therapy session?

Although every therapist works slightly differently, most sessions involve exploring what has been happening recently, discussing thoughts, emotions, or situations that feel important and working together towards agreed goals. Some sessions focus on understanding past experiences, while others concentrate on practical strategies for managing current difficulties. Therapy is collaborative, meaning the therapist and client work together to understand problems and identify approaches that are most helpful for that individual.

Therapy vs talking to a friend: what's the difference?

Talking to a trusted friend can provide comfort, reassurance and emotional support, which are all valuable. Therapy differs because it is guided by psychological knowledge, evidence-based approaches and professional training. Therapists are trained to recognise patterns, ask purposeful questions and use techniques that support lasting change, while also maintaining confidentiality and professional boundaries. The goal is not simply to listen, but to help people understand themselves in ways that improve their wellbeing.

Why would I need therapy if I can't point to what's wrong?

Many people seek therapy without being able to identify one specific problem. They may simply notice that they feel overwhelmed, disconnected, stuck, or unlike themselves. Emotional difficulties often develop gradually through a combination of stress, life experiences, personality, and changing circumstances, rather than one obvious event. Not having a clear explanation does not mean your experiences are less valid and therapy can often help clarify what has been difficult and why.

How do I find the right therapist for me?

Finding the right therapist often involves considering both practical factors and personal fit. Things such as the therapist's qualifications, areas of expertise, therapeutic approach, language, and cultural understanding may all influence your experience. Just as importantly, research consistently shows that feeling comfortable, understood and able to build a trusting relationship with your therapist is one of the strongest predictors of positive outcomes. It is normal for this process to take some time and finding a therapist who feels like a good fit is an important part of therapy itself.
